summary: Explains how to use the IDEA encryption algorithm in CMS and S/MIME as another strong choice for symmetric encryption. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This adds one more secret-code method to the list of codes that secure email programs can use.

questions: how to use idea in s/mime
subtitle: Adding IDEA encryption to secure email and messages

tldr.problem: Some organizations use IDEA encryption for their data, but mainstream secure email systems like S/MIME and CMS did not include it as an option, forcing a choice between security preferences and email compatibility.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies the exact algorithm identifiers (OIDs) and procedures needed to add IDEA as a symmetric encryption option for both the message content itself and for encrypting the keys that protect that content.
tldr.outcome: Organizations using IDEA can now enable it in their S/MIME clients, letting them send encrypted email to each other using their preferred encryption method while following standard email protocols.

today: RFC 3058 is Informational, documenting how to add IDEA support to CMS and S/MIME. While IDEA itself remains secure, the encryption landscape has shifted; modern systems more commonly use AES. However, organizations with existing IDEA deployments can use this RFC to maintain compatibility with standard email security protocols.

sections.title: IDEA and Secure Email
sections.content:
IDEA (International Data Encryption Algorithm) is a strong encryption method that some organizations use for protecting sensitive data. CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) is the standard framework for adding encryption to email and other messages. S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) uses CMS to let email clients encrypt and decrypt messages.

However, CMS and S/MIME come with a standard list of encryption algorithms, and IDEA was not on that list. This RFC fills that gap by specifying how to add IDEA to CMS and S/MIME. The RFC provides the technical identifiers and procedures so that email clients can recognize and use IDEA if the organization enables it.
sections.plainLanguage: IDEA is a secret code used by some companies. Email uses CMS, which is like a envelope with a lock. The lock can use many different secret codes, but IDEA was not one of them. This document says how to add IDEA as a lock option.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers and Encryption Modes
sections.content:
In CMS, each encryption algorithm is identified by a unique object identifier (OID), which is a string of numbers that acts like a registered name. When the RFC specifies a new algorithm, it reserves an OID.

For IDEA encryption, the RFC defines two OIDs: one for encrypting the message content itself (called IDEA-CBC) and one for encrypting the encryption key (called id-alg-CMSIDEAwrap). IDEA-CBC uses cipher block chaining (CBC) mode with a fixed key length of 128 bits. This size is not adjustable; all IDEA keys are exactly 128 bits long.

When the content is encrypted with IDEA-CBC, an initialization vector (IV) is used (an 8-byte random value that varies the encryption so the same plaintext produces different ciphertext each time). The IV can be included in the message parameters or assumed to be the first 8 bytes of the ciphertext.
sections.plainLanguage: Each secret code gets a number ID so the email system knows which one is being used. IDEA gets two numbers: one for locking the message and one for locking the key that unlocks the message. IDEA uses very long secret keys (128 bits) and always uses them the same way.

sections.title: Key Wrapping and Unwrapping
sections.content:
In CMS, there are two separate encryption keys: the content-encryption key (CEK), which encrypts the actual message, and the key-encryption key (KEK), which encrypts the CEK so that the CEK itself can be transmitted securely. The process of encrypting the CEK with the KEK is called key wrapping.

The RFC specifies how IDEA key wrapping works. The algorithm takes the 16-byte CEK, computes an 8-byte checksum, concatenates them, adds a random initialization vector, and encrypts the result using IDEA in CBC mode. The output is then reversed byte-by-byte and encrypted again with a fixed initialization vector. This two-stage process protects against tampering.

Key unwrapping reverses these steps: decrypt with the fixed IV, reverse the bytes, decrypt with the random IV, verify the checksum, and extract the original key. If the checksum does not match, unwrapping fails, indicating the key was corrupted or tampered with.
sections.plainLanguage: The message key is locked with another key. IDEA locks the message key in two stages: shake it up, reverse it, lock it again. Unlocking is the reverse: unlock, un-reverse, shake it again, and check nothing got broken.

sections.title: S/MIME Capabilities and Client Support
sections.content:
An S/MIME client announces what encryption methods it can use by including a S/MIME capabilities attribute in its signed messages. This list tells other clients what algorithms the sender supports, so they can choose a method both sides understand.

If a client supports IDEA encryption, it MUST include the IDEA-CBC OID in the symmetric algorithms section of its capabilities list, and it MUST include the id-alg-CMSIDEAwrap OID in the key encipherment section. The RFC provides the exact hexadecimal encoding of these capabilities.

For IDEA to be used in practice, it must be activated in user preferences on both the sending and receiving clients. The sender's client checks the recipient's capabilities list to see if IDEA is supported. If both sides support IDEA and the user has configured it, encrypted messages can use IDEA.
sections.plainLanguage: When you send a signed email, you also send a list saying 'I can lock with IDEA, AES, and DES'. When the other person wants to send you a locked message, they check your list and pick one you both support.

sections.title: IDEA Security and Standards Status
sections.content:
IDEA was developed jointly by the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology and Ascom Ltd. as a replacement for the aging DES algorithm. It uses 128-bit keys and encrypts one 64-bit block at a time. The full 8-round IDEA has no known attack better than trying all 128-bit keys (exhaustive search).

IDEA is particularly strong against differential cryptoanalysis, a technique used to break many encryption methods. The algorithm has been entered into the ISO/IEC register of encryption algorithms and is approved for use in EDI (Electronic Data Interchange) applications.

Ascom holds the patent for IDEA but offers a non-exclusive license under reasonable, non-discriminatory terms. Non-commercial use is free. Any organization wishing to use IDEA commercially should contact Ascom for licensing information.
sections.plainLanguage: IDEA is a very strong secret code. Mathematicians tried hard to break it and failed. The company that owns it lets people use it for free if it is not for business, or cheaply if it is.
